sections.heading: What the rewrite changes
sections.body:
AI drafts often share the same habits. Most sentences are about the same length. Openers repeat. Stock phrases like "overall, it is clear that" or "it is worth noting" show up where a plain word would do, and the rhythm sounds the same from the first line to the last.

This tool rewrites your text to fix those habits. It mixes short and long sentences, swaps stiff wording for plain words, and cuts filler. The result sounds like someone talking to a reader, not a template filling in blanks.

sections.heading: What it keeps
sections.body:
The rewrite keeps the meaning and the facts in your text. Names, dates, figures and claims should come out the same as they went in.

Still, **read the result before you use it.** A rewrite can change a word that mattered. Only you know exactly what your text needs to say, so check it against the original.

sections.heading: How to use it
sections.body:
The steps are the same on any computer or phone with a browser:

1. Paste your AI-written text into the box, or upload a file up to 15 MB.
2. Run the rewrite. The result usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.
3. Read the new version, check the facts, then copy it with one click.

sections.heading: Free limits
sections.body:
You get 3 free runs a day. Leave an email and you get 3 more that day. You do not need an account to start.

If you run out, the limit resets the next day, so you can finish the rest of your text then.

sections.heading: Check the result before you use it
sections.body:
A humanizer changes how the writing sounds. It does not make the ideas yours, and it does not check whether they are true.

Compare the rewrite with your original line by line. Look for changed numbers, dropped qualifiers such as "usually" or "in most cases", and names spelled differently. If a sentence no longer says what you meant, edit it by hand. That edit is the part that makes the text yours.

sections.heading: Who it is for
sections.body:
This tool is for anyone who has a draft from an AI model that reads flat: students, bloggers, marketers, small business owners and people writing emails at work.

If your text already sounds like you, you probably do not need it. A humanizer is most useful on a draft you are going to publish or send under your own name.

sections.heading: What to check in any AI humanizer
sections.body:
Use the same three tests for every tool you try:

- **Meaning.** Do names, numbers, dates and claims match the original?
- **Sound.** Read it out loud. Does it sound like a person talking, or like a different robot?
- **Limits and cost.** How many free runs do you get, and what do you have to give up to get more?

A tool that passes all three for your kind of writing is the right one for you, even if someone else ranks it lower.

sections.heading: Why no tool can promise undetectable text
sections.body:
Some humanizer sites say their output will get past every AI detector. Nobody can back that up. Detectors are unreliable and make mistakes in both directions: they flag human writing as AI, and they miss AI writing.

OpenAI learned this the hard way. In July 2023 it withdrew its own AI text classifier because its accuracy was too low. If a company that builds AI models could not make a reliable detector, be careful with any humanizer that claims a guaranteed bypass rate.

Judge a humanizer by the writing it gives you, not by a score it promises.

sections.heading: How to test a humanizer on your own text
sections.body:
Run the same paragraph through two or three tools and compare:

1. Pick one paragraph you wrote with AI, with at least a few facts or names in it.
2. Run it through each tool once.
3. Check every fact and name against the original. Note any change.
4. Read each version out loud and pick the one that sounds most like you.

A tool that changes a fact is out, however natural it sounds.

Use your own reading of the text as the test. Would a reader notice the AI habits? If not, the rewrite did its job.

A score can still be useful as a second opinion, but it should never decide whether the text is good.

sections.heading: What it does to an essay draft
sections.body:
An AI draft often reads flat. The sentences match in length, the openers repeat, and the wording is safe. This tool rewrites a paragraph so the sentences vary, the words are plainer and the filler goes. It keeps the meaning and facts.

It does not add research, sources or new ideas. A humanizer changes how the essay sounds. It does not change what you argue or where your evidence comes from.

sections.heading: Check your school's AI rules first
sections.body:
Schools and teachers set their own rules for AI use. Some allow it with disclosure, some do not allow it for certain assignments, and some ask you to write every word yourself. Read your course policy before you paste any essay text into a tool.

If you are not sure whether a use is allowed, ask your teacher before you submit. A humanizer does not change who is responsible for the work you hand in.

If your school asks you to disclose AI use, write down which tools you used and for which paragraphs. Keeping that record takes a minute and saves an argument later.

sections.heading: Steps for one essay paragraph
sections.body:
1. Write the paragraph with your sources in front of you.
2. Paste the paragraph into the tool and run the rewrite.
3. Check every claim, quote and citation against your sources.
4. Edit back any sentence that lost meaning, and add a line in your own voice.

Do the paragraphs one at a time. That makes the fact check easier, and it keeps the essay sounding like one writer.

When the whole essay is done, read it from the top. Check that the introduction still matches the conclusion and that each paragraph still leads into the next one.

sections.heading: Common problems to fix
sections.body:
- A quote that was changed, even slightly. Put the original words back.
- A citation or source number that moved. Match it to your reference list.
- A hedge that got dropped, so the claim now sounds stronger than your evidence.
- A sentence that reads smoothly but says less. Rewrite it so it makes your point again.
